newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov says green bond funds won't be diverted.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov says green bond funds won't be diverted.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki, who wants to ensure his environmental bond is not rejected by voters like one offered by his predecessor, on Monday defended his plan from charges it might pay for questionable projects.

"It's just not the case," Pataki told reporters at a news conference that was held at City Hall. "This is a very clearly focused bond act," he added, noting the referendum, which voters will approve or reject at the November 5 polls, lists specific programs to clean up the state's air, land and water.

While a coalition of 35 environmental groups, the New York League of Conservation Voters, supports the plan, along with the Business Council of New York State and other groups, five local environmental groups criticized the plan.

Saying the bond act's language was too broad, Mary Bentstock, executive director of the Clean Air Campaign, a non-profit environmental group, said "The broad categories voters will be approving if they sign a $1.75 billion blank check in November would authorize decades of wasteful spending on projects which do nothing for clean air or water."

Her prepared comments echoed statements made last week by Change-NY, anti-tax lobbyists, which last week was quoted by the Albany Times Union as saying the act could include a variety of questionable projects. As examples, it listed parking facilities, golf courses and roads.

However, a spokesman for the campaign for the bond act refuted such criticisms, noting the legislature and the governor each year would have to approve the specific projects that would be funded. "The intention was to write very broad categories...It'll be decided on environmental and public concerns."

As much as $275 million of bonds could be approved in 1996, assuming the voters approve the act and Pataki and the legislature agree on a list of programs at a special session that likely will be held after the November 5 elections.

The state comptroller, saluting the Pataki Administration's decision to submit the plan to the voters, said this was the only way to ensure the monies raised by selling the bonds were used solely for the environment.
"By providing funds, funds that can only be used for the environment, voters are ensured that the funds are going to be used for their intended purposes," McCall said.

Saying he hopes the green bond act would mark the start of a trend away from "backdoor" financing, he added that the state stands to save money by issuing general obligation debt while rebuilding its infrastructure.
